content: Cineole, also known as eucalyptol, is a naturally occurring organic compound that exists as a colorless liquid. It is classified as a cyclic ether and a monoterpenoid. This compound is referred to by several synonyms, including 1,8-cineol, 1,8-cineole, cajeputol, 1,8-epoxy-p-menthane, 1,8-oxido-p-menthane, eucalyptole, 1,3,3-trimethyl-2-oxabicyclooctane, cineol, and cineole. The name eucalyptol was first assigned by S. Cloez, who identified it as the primary component of the essential oil derived from Eucalyptus globulus. It is important to distinguish eucalyptus oil, a general term for oils extracted from the Eucalyptus genus, from the specific chemical compound eucalyptol. Eucalyptol constitutes up to 90% of the essential oil in certain species of eucalyptus oil, which is why the compound is commonly associated with this name. Beyond eucalyptus, eucalyptol is also present in other aromatic plants, such as camphor laurel, bay leaves, tea tree, mugwort, sweet basil, wormwood, rosemary, common sage, and Cannabis sativa. It can be extracted in significant quantities—up to 8%—through fractional distillation of eucalyptus oil. While eucalyptol is used in small doses as a flavoring agent and medicinal ingredient, it is toxic when ingested in higher-than-normal amounts, a characteristic shared with many essential oils. Eucalyptol has a fresh, camphor-like aroma and a spicy, cooling taste. It is insoluble in water but can mix with ether, ethanol, and chloroform. Its boiling point is 176°C, and its flash point is 49°C. The compound forms crystalline adducts with halogen acids, o-cresol, resorcinol, and phosphoric acid, which are useful for its purification. Uses of Eucalyptol Flavoring and Fragrance Eucalyptol is widely used in flavorings, fragrances, and cosmetics due to its pleasant spicy aroma and taste. It is incorporated in trace amounts (e.g., 0.002%) in products such as baked goods, confectionery, meat products, and beverages. In a 1994 report by major cigarette manufacturers, eucalyptol was listed as one of the 599 additives used in cigarettes, where it is claimed to enhance flavor. Medicinal Applications Eucalyptol is a common ingredient in various brands of mouthwash and cough suppressants. It is also used as an inactive ingredient in body powders. Insecticide and Repellent Eucalyptol serves as an insecticide and insect repellent. Interestingly, it is also one of the compounds that attract male orchid bees, which collect the chemical to synthesize pheromones. This property makes eucalyptol a useful bait for studying these bees. Toxicology At doses higher than normal, eucalyptol is hazardous when ingested, inhaled, or comes into contact with the skin. Acute exposure can affect behavior, the respiratory tract, and the nervous system. The acute oral LD50 for rats is 2480 mg/kg. Eucalyptol is classified as a reproductive toxin for females and a suspected reproductive toxin for males. Scientific Studies A 2003 study demonstrated that eucalyptol could control airway mucus hypersecretion and asthma. Earlier research by the same authors found that eucalyptol suppresses arachidonic acid metabolism and cytokine production in human monocytes. A 2004 study showed that eucalyptol inhibits cytokine production in cultured human lymphocytes and monocytes. Another 2004 study found eucalyptol to be an effective treatment for nonpurulent rhinosinusitis. Patients experienced reduced symptoms such as frontal headache, nasal obstruction, rhinological secretion, and sensitivity at trigeminal nerve pressure points. Side effects were minimal. A 2000 study revealed that topical application of eucalyptol reduces inflammation and pain. A 2002 study found that eucalyptol selectively killed leukemia cells in two human leukemia cell lines in vitro, while sparing cells from a human stomach cancer cell line. Eucalyptol is listed as cineole in certain pharmacopoeias.
